title: The First Vending Machine Sold Holy Water 2,000 Years Ago 🪙 #shorts
description:
The earliest known coin-operated vending machine was described by the Greek engineer Heron (Hero) of Alexandria in the 1st century AD. Temple visitors dropped in a five-drachma coin, which tipped a small lever, opened a valve and released a portion of holy water until the coin slid off. Modern coin machines only caught on in London in the 1880s, selling postcards – and today Japan alone has nearly 4 million vending machines.

Sources: Smithsonian (via Mental Floss), Smith College, Sky HISTORY, 99% Invisible, Gizmodo, Japan Vending System Manufacturers Association (via Statista/SoraNews24)

scenes.text: The first vending machine didn't sell snacks. It sold holy water, almost two thousand years ago.
scenes.headline:
ANCIENT
VENDING
MACHINE

scenes.text: It was designed by Heron, a Greek engineer in Alexandria, Egypt, in the first century.
The problem? Temple visitors kept taking more holy water than they paid for.
So Heron's machine took a coin. The price for one portion: five drachmas.
scenes.label: ONE PORTION

scenes.text: The coin landed on a tiny tray on a lever. The tray tipped, a valve opened, and water flowed.
When the coin slid off, the valve closed again. No electricity at all.
Modern coin machines only caught on in London in the eighteen eighties, selling postcards.
Today, Japan alone has nearly four million vending machines.
scenes.label: MILLION IN JAPAN
